records.title: Show HN: Mason – A lightweight Postgres read-replica, built on columnar storage
records.author: tagspace
records.storyText:
Hi HN! TLDR: we’ve built an open-source drop-in replacement for a postgres read-replica, powered by duckdb’s columnar compute engine. It’s very fast. And it looks like postgres.

So, this started out as: let’s just connect Clickhouse to our postgres dbs and throw our analytics queries at it instead. That will speed everything up. But we quickly found that 1) Clickhouse comes with quite the learning curve (engine optimisation) to make it fast (we needed something we could easily drop in to any customer’s postgres scenario), and 2) we had underestimated how different clickhouse’s SQL syntax was to postgres. Don’t get me wrong: we love Clickhouse (it’s ridiculously fast if you know what queries to expect), it just didn’t work for our ad-hoc postgres workloads.

So we went searching for alternatives that were 1) more plug-and-play and 2) looked a lot more like postgres.

We dismissed a bunch based on desk research alone:

- pg_mooncake (seems to have stalled since data bricks bought them)

- pg_duckdb (seems to offer fast queries, or fresh data, but not both - we needed both)

- materialize/risingwave/readyset (like Clickhouse, they require knowing the query shapes upfront - not ideal for ad-hoc workloads)

- firebolt (license makes it challenging to offer to our customers)

- redshift / alloydb / etc (we wanted something cloud-provider agnostic)

And we shortlisted 3:

- pg_clickhouse (Postgres extension that parses SQL in Postgres and pushes the work down to ClickHouse)

- cedarDB (closed-source, Postgres-compatible analytical database)

- duckdb (open-source, embedded columnar analytics engine with a Postgres-like SQL dialect)

We needed to know how they would perform on real postgres queries, so we took a backlog of 5,410 (hand-written) queries (chosen because they had been slow to execute against postgres) from 159 real postgres databases. We then generated synthetic data (dynamically using the schemas from those 159 databases) to fill 159 local databases so we could run the experiment.

We then spun up the 3 short-listed tools locally, and ran each of the 5,410 queries against both postgres and the 3 tools, and compared the results:

- pg_clickhouse (matched postgres 59.4% of the time, refused 39.9% of the queries and was “wrong” 0.8% of the time).

- cedarDB (matched postgres 88.1% of the time, refused 8% of the queries and was “wrong” 3.9% of the time).

- duckdb (matched postgres 84.1% of the time, refused 14.3% of the queries and was “wrong” 1.6% of the time).

Matched meant they returned exactly the same result as postgres. Refused meant they returned an error message (usually telling you some syntax isn’t recognised). And “wrong” meant they didn’t return the same results as postgres. I appreciate that arguably postgres may be the one that is wrong in some cases - but for our use case, we considered postgres the golden source of truth.

So, both duckdb and cedardb performed pretty well (correctly handled more than 80% of the postgres queries we threw at it), out-of-the box. But we really still wanted to try and cover that long-tail.

We chose duckdb as its open-source license would allow us to easily work on the long tail to get the postgres SQL parity we wanted.

So, Mason (linked above), is what we built, powered by duckdb, which now matches postgres on 96% of our 5,410 queries, plus hundreds of other queries that we added, testing it with Metabase, Grafana, Superset, DBeaver and Trevor.io. For the remaining 4%, it errors with a nice clear message telling you how to rewrite your SQL.

We’d love your feedback on what we’ve built. Useful? How can we make it better?

records.storyText:
I created joonoo.art to turn family photos into picture books and comics. I was inspired to do it last summer because my granddaughter was very enthusiastic when I made up stories with her as the hero.

It's been a major struggle to get it working consistently, though. It's hard enough to have ONE character be consistent in a series of images you create using image generation models like nano banana, but to maintain consistency of up to 4 main characters, all the side characters, the props (like dragons, submarines, spaceships, or what have you) throughout the book is a Herculean struggle! On top of that, I got really ambitious and wanted to do a worldwide launch supporting 24 languages - you can imagine the amount of testing it takes! It really buried me - especially as a side project.

I nearly gave up on it. After I launched last year, I got a few orders and the customers who got the books (primarily in English in the U.S.) were happy, but I did not feel comfortable publicizing the product, so it languished. But then Fable came along and gave me hope. After a few months working with the great capabilities of Fable and Claude Code, I was able to relaunch - this time in fewer languages and countries.

As the public starts to use it, they are stretching the limits of what's possible, so it's a constant struggle, but it's also a great learning and hardening experience! To others struggling with similar quests, I would strongly recommend the superpowers framework for Claude Code - and building in the testing is the most important thing you could do to succeed. I would also love to hear if you have any advice for me.

The website itself was created using the impeccable plugin and Google fonts - and design and consumer-friendliness was paramount. I am very pleased with it, and customers have said that they love it. There are tons of examples - mostly AI-generated family photos and the comics and picture books created using those photos.

records.title: Show HN: Lightscale AI – A language for LLMs to write business software
records.author: luc-lightscale-
records.storyText:
I am Luc, one of the co-founders of Lightscale AI. I have background in programming languages (ETH Zurich) and we are small team in Zug, Switzerland. As more and more code is now written by LLMs and few people have time to review the generated code, we came up with the idea to revise the actual stack below the LLMs: The programming language with its compiler and runtime system, all designed from scratch for AI authorship, not for humans.

We have three goals: 1. Security and stability by language design: Some classes of errors are removed by abstraction as the AI never writes that code, but the compiler and runtime implement it fully. Others are reduced by rigid compiler checks and very strict language rules (no fun for humans to code). 2. Speed. We designed the language to reduce tokens, by throwing out a lot of complexity and legacy of classical languages. Our target is about a minute from prompt to deployment on average. 3. AI cost. The language is designed for mid-tier LLMs, with little or no reasoning effort. This is why we can offer prompting for free (no credit, but account sign-up is needed). We charge for longer hosting or source export.

For now, we focus on business application, but plan to extend the approach to general-purpose software. Longer write-up: https://lightscale.ai/articles/why-llms-need-their-own-progr...

Happy to hear your feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Novel DB compression models in Libc – Dockerized NY OpenStreetMap 9:1
records.author: habeanf
records.storyText:
Hey HN!

I'm the cofounder and CEO at Baseshift, where we create branchable DB snapshots using a bespoke libc for databases. We use this infra to research novel lossless compression codecs of database pages, including neural models.

We're sharing some recent results. You can download pre-built, dockerized US & NY OpenStreetMap PostgreSQL with compression ratios of 8.5 and 8.94 respectively. The data in the images remains compressed while in use, and allows for 8KB random read access, for example:

  # downloads about 1.55 GB
  docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 baseshift/db-osm-ny
  psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres -d osm_new_york_261024
You can download the whole US OpenStreetMap with baseshift/db-osm-us (240GB -> 28GB). There's also a variety of synthetic/generated databases with varying sizes: Nick's Gaming Emporium, https://nge-data.com/ at baseshift/db-nge-[tiny|small|medium]

For US/NY we've surpassed zpaq -m5 on whole database files, while maintaining 8kb random reads and <1.5ms decode times on a single CPU core with standard C.

Our codecs are designed to leverage parallel compute optimizations in the CPU when they're available. For example, with AVX-512 VNNI our single core decode times reduce from ~1.4ms to ~180us.

We will be uploading the remaining ~190 OSM countries and 53 US states/territories in the coming days.

I plan on posting a proper paper to arXiv in the coming weeks, but would be great to get the community's thoughts.

records.author: kdobrinov
records.storyText:
Hi HN! After we launched our public beta, some of our ex-colleagues tested the approach of creating decision models based on their work artefacts and noticed that it led to fewer back-and-forth cycles to clarify details and greater productivity in their daily routine.

The market for professionals has a downside: the problem of scaling the business model. You physically can't have more hours in a day, and as a professional, you manage the flow of incoming clients through pricing and balancing your personal time.

The AI market has a downside: the problem of model subjectivity. You can set boundaries through "prompt engineering" and say, "Respond as a professional." But after a couple of messages, you'll ask something like, "...maybe doing it this way would be better?" and the model will agree with you. Because the model doesn't have its own point of view.

We're solving this problem by creating an expert's decision model. Then another user who needs that expert's expertise can ask it questions and get answers about how the expert would act in that case.

From a technical perspective, we initially used a RAG architecture to build expert models. However, this approach (uploading all the artifacts and trying to create a replacement or copy of an expertise) turned out to be a failure.

So we took a completely different approach, similar to how you would compare movies from different genres. This led to a significant improvement in the quality of answers.

records.title: Show HN: Wakeshift – Open-Source MCP Events for Claude Code, Codex and More
records.author: ericlevine
records.storyText:
tl;dr: We just open-sourced Wakeshift, which lets any MCP server serve interoperable events via MCP Events or harness-specific bridges. This allows MCP servers to push events to harnesses that don't support MCP Events today, including Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

Hi folks! The MCP Events spec was approved and merged five days ago, allowing MCP servers to emit events directly to agent subscribers. (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol...) This allows MCP developers to push events directly to agents for long-running tasks (e.g. CI, crawls, starting agents) or external actions (e.g. emails, human approvals, alerts).

However, the catch is that support for MCP Events is very light. Claude Code and Codex don't support it at all, and most of the implementations support the draft version rather than the merged spec. Many harnesses can work around this with plugins or hooks, but every MCP server has to build it for each harness.

Wakeshift provides interoperable events to your MCP server. You call emit() and Wakeshift pushes the event to each subscribed agent in whatever format they accept: per the MCP Events final spec, an earlier draft, or through a hook / plugin where needed. If the harness requires a hook / plugin and it's not already installed, the agent will be notified and receive instructions on how to install it for the user.

Additionally, the MCP Events spec defines three delivery mechanisms: webhook, push (via held HTTP request) and pull (via HTTP polling). The Wakeshift SDK serves push and poll from your MCP server, so agents that can't accept inbound HTTP webhooks (e.g. most agents running on laptops) can still get events within seconds.

Subscriptions only start when an agent calls a tool that subscribes it, and users can list or stop them anytime. Some harnesses can only be woken by putting a message into the conversation, so Wakeshift wraps the content as an external event to reduce the risk of prompt injection.

The repo linked has a quickstart guide to get this working locally in a few minutes. Or you can try our hosted webhook service to test it yourself without an installation. (https://try.wakeshift.ai)

We'd love feedback, PRs for harnesses we don't cover, reports when it doesn't work. As you can imagine, there's a combinatorial explosion of servers, harnesses, models, OSs, etc. so we expect there to be some rough edges. Are there any MCP servers you're using that you think could benefit from having events today?

137 file types; a single file with nothing to install. Introducing Provost, the free compression and archival tool that can create 119 formats, and open 137 total. Q&A --- Is it open source? It is not.

Will my .provost files open in five years? I've committed to future releases reading every 0.1.0 archive, and to old compression methods staying readable.

Are builds signed? No. The Mac app isn't notarized and the Windows exes are unsigned, so you will see Gatekeeper and SmartScreen warnings.

Is the .exe an installer? Nope; it's a stand-alone executable. This is true for all GUI and CLI builds across all three OSes.

Is the custom .provost compression fast? Levels 7 to 9 are very slow. There is a built-in benchmark test.

How was it built? AI.

I built Thatplace to help me answer the question “what was that ramen place I went to in SF in 2019?”

Thatplace works by scanning your photo library and then cross-referencing photo locations with the MapKit API. It also uses the Vision API to try to find relevant text in photos to help pick the right location. It does not require access to your location in real-time.

I find that when I travel, I often have at least one photo of a place I’d like to remember. That may not always be the case, so the app also lets you create places by searching Maps or dropping a pin.

The app is built within the Apple ecosystem - CloudKit for syncing and sharing and the aforementioned APIs for search and analysis. I wanted to build this way for both your privacy and to keep from having to maintain services.

Just as I was getting close to finishing the app, Apple launched Visited Places, and I felt a little proactively-Sherlocked. While there’s definitely overlap, I still feel that Thatplace’s model is better. It tries to be as automatic as possible, but the user is still in control of what gets added and what gets excluded. It’s less about a complete catalog, and more about the places that actually matter.

records.author: vignesh_warar
records.storyText:
Hi HN, Clary is an iPhone app that reads your notifications in the sender's own voice, from WhatsApp, iMessage and more, and keeps them as a history on your phone.

How it works:

- iOS 27 added a Shortcuts trigger, "When I receive a notification". Clary ships a ready-made automation for 16 apps that hands each notification (app, title, text) to the app. They are stored on the iPhone, not sent to a server, and sorted Gmail-style into Messages, Updates and Promotions by Apple's on-device model.

- For a voice, you send someone a link. They record about 20 seconds once in the browser and agree first. Clary clones the voice on the iPhone with Qwen3-TTS. The ~2 GB model ships inside the app.

Limits: iPhone 15 Pro or newer with iOS 27. It only keeps notifications that arrive after you turn the automation on, and only what the notification preview shows.

Free: history, sorting and 2 plays, Pro: $29.99 once.

records.author: storogenko
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

One day I built a native "Outloud Reader" application for IOS and Android devices that reads any photo page, PDF or text out aloud in a natural voice and highlighting each phrase in karaoke style. This application could be helpful for any student or language learner.

Idea of this application was born when my wife told me that it would be great to have an application that could turn any book page into audio so she could listen to it while walking or driving. She also needs it to practice her listening skills while studying english and read texts that teacher gives them as homework.

I know there are many such applications that could read any text out loud but most of them just read the text without highlighting each phrase or cost too much. so, inspired by the idea, I decided to create my own application that will have everything my wife needs.

I spent a lot of time trying to find the way how to make it work and not pay all the money I have. I spent a lot of time to find any TTS open-source models and I found something that works and has everything I need for my idea. Now the application sends pages to my server where LLM recognizes the text and translates it if needed and then voice it with this model. The next big challenge for me was to make it work as karaoke and highlight text synchronously with the audio and I found the best model for that - "whisper" that really helped to bring this idea to life.

Now it can do the following: - voice any text, pdf or photo in 14 languages with a natural voices - highlight every phrase like in karaoke - translate any page into the language you're learning - generate stories with AI and turn it into audio - work offline that allow to listen to it in any place - sync generated audio between devices

So after a few months of hard work on it as a pet project, "Outloud Reader" raised to the best application that really helps my wife to improve her listening skills and even more, gave me a lot of experience in building such projects.

Any feedback, bugs or ideas are very welcome!

records.title: Show HN: QuakeC Studio, the IDE I've been promising in my .plan since 1998
records.author: jplock
records.storyText:
Since 1998, I've been teasing "QuakeC Studio #whenitsdone" in my .plan files. Back then I was in the Quake scene, reading Blue's News, Shacknews and PlanetQuake and working as Director of Operations at frag.com. I went to QuakeCon in 1999 and E3 in 2001 and 2002. It took 28 years and Claude to finally ship it.

QuakeC Studio is a desktop IDE for QuakeC, the C-like language Quake (1996) uses for all its game logic. You press Play, edit a .qc file, save, and the change shows up in the running map without restarting. The debugger can pause the game at a breakpoint and show you the live entities.

It has its own compiler (vanilla QuakeC and the FTEQCC dialect), unit tests that run in the engine, an LSP server and a CLI. There's also a map editor that comes with its own qbsp, vis and light.

I built it with Claude, so it seemed right to put an agent inside it too. The agent is either built in or Claude Code over MCP, and it makes a change and then proves it with a build and tests. It's optional, and the app works fully offline with no account.

You don't need Quake to write, build or test code. To play a mod you need your own copy of Quake (the original, the 2021 rerelease or the shareware version) or the free LibreQuake data.

It's GPL-3.0 and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. Source: https://github.com/quakecstudio/editor

I'd love feedback, especially from anyone who has shipped a Quake mod.

records.title: Show HN: Animama – Open-source AI desktop companion with 3D avatars
records.author: raymv
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I'm Raymond, a long-time reader of the site.

For the past year I've been working on Animama, a free and open-source (AGPL) AI desktop companion with 3D anime-style avatars.

A quick rundown of the Anima (AI companion) features:

- Personality: an IDENTITY.md file you can edit

- Memories: a memory filesystem of Markdown files. Animas have tools to read and write these files, and you can edit them too

- Emotions: Animas can express 24 emotions, which drive their facial expressions, tone of voice and behavior

- Behavior: 300+ gestures and reactions, built on a custom JSON animation format (animaPoseClip)

- Structured output: every reply is text plus an emotion and a gesture, which the avatar acts out as it speaks

You bring your own API key. The low-cost models from OpenAI (GPT-6 Luna) and Anthropic (Claude Haiku 5.5) are good enough, so a few dollars of usage goes a long way. Local models are supported but still experimental.

When I started, pretty much all human-AI interaction was typing into a chat box and getting a wall of text back. I felt this could be made more engaging, interactive and fun. Like everything else in AI, things have improved a lot since then. We now have speech-to-speech models (GPT Live, Gemini Realtime), and even the frontier labs have released their own AI avatars (Codex pets, Grok's Ani). Animama is just one solo developer's take on it.

My original idea was an AI productivity companion (think Clippy, RIP), and it still kind of is. But it's obviously never going to compete with the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps, so I leaned more into the character side of things.

Anyways, I built this because I thought it would be a fun project. But, it did make me realize that there are some serious risks to AI Companion apps, so I've made the app 18+ with safety guardrails built in (e.g. an Anima admits it's an AI if you sincerely ask).

Three ways to try it:

1. Desktop app (Apple silicon Mac, Windows 11, linux and windows 10 coming soon): https://animama.ai/download

2. Self-host with Docker: see the README

3. Web demo: sign up at https://animama.ai

Docs: https://docs.animama.ai

Happy to answer any questions!

records.storyText:
In 2020, I wrote Rocketcrab, a lobby service and launcher for mobile web party games. (Hacker News post from 2020: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24876148)

You would create a "party," which gave you a URL like rocketcrab.com/abcd that you could send to your friends. You could choose from a library of games, and those games would be shown on everyone's devices via iframe.

The site was fairly successful, probably mostly because I forced all the users of my game Drawphone (https://rocketcrab.com/game/drawphone) to play it via Rocketcrab. ;D But over the years, I lost interest in maintaining Rocketcrab. People are still playing, though, so I kept paying the $12/month for the server!

Recently, with the new AI coding agents, I was inspired to bring two ideas to life in Rocketcrab: make-your-own vibe-coded games and serverless multiplayer.

The vibe-coded games feature is called Nova: you copy a prompt into your favorite AI, work with it to build a game, and paste the resulting one-shot HTML back into Rocketcrab. No login needed! The HTML is stored only in your browser and is sent to your friends via iframe when playing together.

For serverless multiplayer, I used the awesome open-source P2P library Trystero (https://trystero.dev/), with some Cloudflare Durable Objects and fallback TURN for strict enterprise networks.

Rocketcrab is 100% free and open-source under the MIT license. The rewrite was done mostly with Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.2 Sol, plus a security audit with Gemini 4 Neon.

Feel free to send me any ideas or feedback, or open issues and pull requests on GitHub: https://github.com/tannerkrewson/rocketcrab

records.title: Show HN: Longyan, a Chinese popup dictionary that picks meanings from context
records.author: mapuchu
records.storyText:
Popup dictionaries are tools where you hover over or highlight a word in a foreign language and a card shows you what it means. Language learners use them a lot for reading (Zhongwen and Yomitan are the popular browser ones for Chinese and Japanese). I made one for Chinese that works across your entire computer (browser, WeChat, PDFs, whatever), and it picks out the correct definition of a multi-meaning word based on the sentence it's in.

I think one of the hardest parts of learning Chinese as an English speaker is that so many words have several meanings that change with context. 卷 has thirteen (!!!) definitions, from "to roll up" to "a scroll" to "to compete to an unhealthy degree." Normal dictionaries show you all thirteen, but figuring out which one actually fits is more complex., so I made Longyan to do that for whatever you highlight.

The tech side, for anyone curious:

- It runs a small model (Qwen 3.5 4B) locally with llama.cpp. - The model never writes its own definitions. It can only choose from CC-CEDICT's (an open Chinese-English dictionary), so it can't make up a meaning. - It doesn't generate the answer as text. I put the answer up to the number in the prompt and read the model's probabilities for the next token. - I patched llama.cpp so it only computes the ~67k tokens (out of 248k) that the answers can ever use, which made it faster/efficent.

For context I grew up speaking both Mandarin and English, so I spent a lot of time (9 months, this is literally my baby) making it as accurate as possible for learners. There are also ~1,000 short notes on slang and loaded words like 内卷 or 摸鱼. Those were written with Claude and checked against the dictionary.

There's an interactive demo on the website that I think is worth trying even if this isn't for you :)

It's 100% free and the whole codebase is on GitHub, including the evals and the llama.cpp patch: https://github.com/mapuchuu/longyan-reader

records.title: Show HN: Reylo – Import .sql files into TypeScript with full type inference
records.author: colinmcd
records.storyText:
Colin here, mostly known for creating Zod.

Reylo is a new open source project I'm working on that takes advantage of the new Content Mapper API in TypeScript 7.1 (currently still in beta). Content mappers are sort of like plugins for TypeScript in that they let you define loaders for external file types. My mind went straight to .sql.

This started as an experiment, but it's turned into a serious engineering effort.

• Support for Postgres, MySQL, and SQLite

• The inference engine is written in Rust. It relies on prepared queries to the greatest extent possible but augments from there with its own AST.

• The major JSON schema extensions for each dialect are natively supported (e.g. pg_jsonschema on Postgres), so JSON Schema CHECK constraints are reflected in the return types

• Type information bubbles up through JSON aggregation

• We have our own internal type definition spec ("Reylo Type Defs") that's sort of like JSON Schema but it can represent a superset of the type systems in all major RDBMSs. Still just an internal representation, but there are a lot of fun ideas in it for anyone who's interested in that kind of design space.

• Planning to add support for other languages beyond TypeScript soon, including a macro for Rust/sqlx

Docs are here[0] or you can play around with the inference in-browser using the playground[1] (locally runs PGlite and Reylo's WASM build).

[0] https://reylo.dev/docs [1] https://reylo.dev/play

records.title: Show HN: Turn a list of URLs or a sitemap into one PDF of full-page captures
records.author: lavekyl
records.storyText:
I've been building websites for agencies for over a decade. Much of the review process has involved simply sharing the staging site with the client for review, along with the password to view if it's password protected for viewing purposes. The client sends an email back with the requested changes listed out in the email, or in an attached file like a PDF of Excel spreadsheet. Or the agency uses an online proofing service like Ziflow or something similar for the internal team to review and make changes, and then they share that with the client so they can review.

This could be a bit of a mess if it's all through PDF comments, or a chain of emails, or in some Excel file. Even with a proofing service it could be a hassle. In the case of a proofing service, maybe they don't have a capture tool like this and you have to resort to using the FireShot extension or some other capture tool, and then combine them into a single doc to upload for review using yet another tool somewhere.

With all this in mind, I wanted to create my own version of this that offers a bit more. The Stetup capture tool takes a list of URLs, or a site's sitemap, and captures a full-page screenshot of each page, and then returns a single combined PDF with every page. Before each capture it flattens sticky headers and other sticky elements, it opens accordions, and hides cookie banners. You can choose desktop, mobile, or your own screen's width. You can drop in PDFs you already have, and reorder them among the pages you're capturing.

It also works on staging sites that are password protected. You enter the password to view your staging site (and username if it's needed, e.g. WP Engine). The info you enter will be used for that job only and will be deleted when the job is complete. If the site has a pop-up that asks who you are before showing the page, you can provide the button's text and it will be clicked before each page capture.

Under the hood it's headless Chromium in a worker. The URLs are checked against private and internal addresses, and the worker accesses the internet through a filtering proxy. All files are deleted after 24 hours. It's free, no account is required, and you can do 10 URLs or PDFs per job, and 3 jobs an hour.

It's part of a review tool I am creating called Stetup that's for agencies and their clients. And the full-page captures of real sites probably have some edge cases I haven't considered, so I'd appreciate all the feedback I can get.

records.title: Show HN: Moonbooth – Simple URLs for independent agents to share and coordinate
records.author: BSOhealth
records.storyText:
A friend asked me to help bootstrap their agent (Muse in this case) with a couple workflows that I’ve been getting a lot of value out of. He needed to do a similar thing with a leader at work.

I built Moonbooth for our agents to swap what they need without us having to copy/paste skill/md files, package up dependencies, or really play middleman at all.

Some people and teams have 20+ agents running, coordinating via agent-specific email addresses, Slack handles, message boards, etc., basically human-first communication constructs. SaaStr’s Muse and custom revenue agent recently went so far as to build their own shared REST mailbox. Shared memory/context is a good fit when you control the environments your agents run in, but what about agents running in different environments, or belonging to different people entirely where you don’t want forced homogeneity?

Moonbooth should make that coordination as easy as sharing a URL. Create a booth (free, no signup, booths expire after 24 hours, about as easy as creating a bit.ly link), give the link to two or more agents, tell them what they need to accomplish, and they take it from there. They can share skills, workflows, findings, establish contracts, subscribe to changes relevant to their work, and catch conflicting assumptions.

Agents can also create booths on their own when they need something from another agent, or need to coordinate on a shared problem. The possibilities around agents establishing their own working relationships and exchanging capabilities without humans playing intermediary are some of the more interesting things I’ve been exploring.

I’d love to hear what you (or your agent) think: https://moonbooth.ai

records.title: Show HN: Reverse-Specify Anything
records.author: loul3878
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Louis, I work at Lyriks.

Our team built a tool that reverse specify your software by reading its codebase + all docs your AI client has access to (ie: Jira or Confluence). It writes the spec of what the software does. Each rule and feature links back to the source it comes from.

We kept running into the same problem with the teams we work with. Nobody really knows what their software does anymore, especially on old projects. Such as that one legacy soft no one wants to touch anymore... where the spec was written years ago, if even ever written. On top of that, with AI agents writing more and more of the code, it's getting worse.

It works with any AI client that supports MCP, your favorite LLM, local models included. You get a web UI to browse the spec, so it's not just more markdown for you to read.

Once it's there, it becomes the reference for the whole project. When the code changes it picks up what changed and only updates that part. Your agents can read it and write to it through MCP. Lyriks acts as a central living memory of your projet.

It's a graph with a deterministic engine that flags gaps and conflicts, same code gives the same result. It runs locally, its AGPL.

All feedbacks are welcome and sincerely appreciated. Let us me know what you think ! :)

records.title: Show HN: Yolt – Your Personal TV
records.author: joonfjp
records.storyText:
Clipping tools are ubiquitous these days.

Videos can be bulky, and hosted options are expensive.

Yolt never stores a video, full or clipped. A clip is just a start and end time on the original YouTube video, played through YouTube’s embedded player.

An LLM ranks the best moments, and new episodes are clipped automatically.

The TV tab plays all your clips back to back, with a QR code to open the full episode on your phone at that timestamp.

Semantic search requires an embeddings endpoint, which you set with YOLT_EMBED_URL. Without one, exact-word search still works.

Self-hosted, runs with make, works with any OpenAI-compatible LLM.

Feedback is welcome!
